claim: Eta-squared and partial eta-squared are biased estimators of population variance explained; epsilon-squared and omega-squared are the less-biased alternatives, per Kelley (1935) and Olejnik & Algina (2003).
stance_target: MANDATORY methodological gap: the AAAI-27 draft reports eta^2_surr and eta^2_opt as its primary effect-size metric throughout, including at n=7 synthetic tasks, without citing the small-sample eta-squared bias literature or reporting omega-squared/epsilon-squared alternatives
scope_conditions: ANOVA-type effect-size estimation, general statistical methodology (R 'effectsize' package documentation, JOSS)
quoted_support: "epsilon_squared() and omega_squared(), which are less biased estimates of the variance explained in the population (T. L. Kelley, 1935; Olejnik & Algina, 2003)."

claim: Olejnik & Algina (2003), 'Generalized Eta and Omega Squared Statistics: Measures of Effect Size for Some Common Research Designs' (Psychological Methods 8:434-447), is the standard-reference paper for eta-squared bias correction, with approximately 1,647 citations per OpenAlex, indicating it is the field's canonical citation for this exact methodological point.
stance_target: establishing the citation weight/authority of the eta-squared-bias literature the AAAI-27 draft omits
quoted_support: OpenAlex record: 'Generalized Eta and Omega Squared Statistics: Measures of Effect Size for Some Common Research Designs' (2003), cited_by_count = 1647.
